notes: Reuben’s firstborn status, Joseph’s birthright, and Judah’s leadership are distinguished rather than treated as the same privilege.
Pul and Tilgath-pilneser are both named in the Hebrew. The wording is retained; these names are associated with the same Assyrian ruler.
vocabulary: Birthright
The standing and inheritance associated with the firstborn.
Unfaithfulness
Betrayal of a binding relationship; the verse also uses the image of prostitution after other gods.

notes: Public 6:1–15 corresponds to Hebrew 5:27–41; public 6:16–81 to Hebrew 6:1–66.
Amminadab is retained here; verse 38 names Izhar in the corresponding ancestry. These lists have not been silently harmonized.
The Hebrew repeats Elkanah and has a written/read difference between “his son” and “sons of.” The difficult sequence is retained.

The Hebrew reads “the firstborn, Vashni, and Abijah.” Many understand a damaged phrase meaning “the firstborn [Joel], and the second, Abijah”; Joel is named in verse 33. The draft retains Vashni and leaves the textual question open.
The list preserves its own town names and totals. Some names and the number of towns actually listed differ from Joshua 21; thirteen in verse 60 is not silently reduced to the eleven named here.
The Hebrew uses the plural “cities of refuge” before each list. Not every following town is identified as a refuge city elsewhere.
The Hebrew wording about tribal families and half of Manasseh is compressed and difficult. Additional tribes have not been inserted.
vocabulary: Atonement
Ritual action addressing sin and impurity so that the relationship with God may be restored.
Pasturelands
Open land attached to a town for its animals and other needs.

notes: Five leaders are stated, though four sons follow Izrahiah’s name. The total may include Izrahiah; the text does not explain it.

The family connections in this passage are uncertain. The relationships involving Asriel, the Aramean concubine, Huppim, Shuppim, Maacah, and the “second” Zelophehad cannot all be settled from this wording.
The pronouns do not clearly identify which group went down to seize whose livestock.
Beriah sounds like the Hebrew phrase “in trouble,” linking the child’s name to the household’s calamity.
Sheerah is explicitly a daughter and is credited with building the three named towns.
The relationship of Resheph to the surrounding names is not fully stated.
vocabulary: Ancestral house
A family group identified through a shared ancestor.
Bilhah
The mother of Dan and Naphtali; see Genesis 30:3–8.

notes: The wording about removal to Manahath and Gera’s part in it is difficult; the event is not otherwise explained here.
The founder or “father” of Gibeon is unnamed in this verse; 9:35 names Jeiel.
Eshbaal and Meribbaal are retained as Chronicles names them. Samuel generally calls them Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth.
Jehoaddah and Raphah here differ from Jarah and Rephaiah in 9:42–43. Both forms remain visible in their own passages.
vocabulary: Fathered
Identifies descent; genealogical lists may span generations.
Bocheru
Retained as a personal name, though the form resembles the word for firstborn.

notes: The settlement notice follows exile in verse 1 and is rendered in that setting.
Shilonites is the Hebrew designation; it is often related to the descendants of Shelah, but the wording has not been replaced.
The unusual expression “house of the tent” connects this gatekeeping description with the tent sanctuary.
This repeated genealogy has its own forms and details, including Ner, Zechariah, Shimeam, Jarah, and Rephaiah. They have not been made identical to chapter 8.
vocabulary: Temple servants
A group assigned to support sanctuary service, distinct here from priests and Levites.
Arranged bread
Bread laid out before God and renewed each Sabbath; also called the bread of the Presence.

notes: The Hebrew can describe trembling or anguish; some understand Saul as wounded by the archers.
“All his house” is retained as this account’s summary. Chapters 8–9 also preserve later descendants of Saul’s family.
Chronicles names a terebinth here; the parallel burial notice in 1 Samuel 31:13 names a tamarisk.
The narrator links Saul’s death to unfaithfulness and seeking a medium rather than the LORD. This judgment remains distinct from the preceding description of his death.
vocabulary: Medium
Someone consulted to communicate with the dead.
Seek
A recurring Chronicles word for turning to God for guidance and help.

notes: The titles and ranks involving the Three and the Thirty are textually difficult. Verse 21 may describe twice the honor, or a second rank; the draft does not collapse all the groups into one.
The field contains barley here; the parallel in 2 Samuel 23:11 mentions lentils.
The Hebrew calls the two Moabite opponents “ariels.” The term may describe formidable warriors, but its precise meaning here is uncertain.
The Egyptian’s height is five cubits. A cubit is the length from elbow to fingertip; ancient standards varied.
vocabulary: Millo
A named fortified structure or earthwork associated with Jerusalem.
Poured out
David treats the water as too closely bound to the men’s endangered lives to drink it, and gives it to the LORD.

notes: This public verse combines Hebrew 12:4–5. Public 12:5–40 then corresponds to Hebrew 12:6–41.
The Hebrew may mean each man was a match for a hundred or a thousand, or that they commanded units of those sizes.
The Spirit “clothed” Amasai: the ancient image is retained. His title can also be understood as chief of officers.
Jozabad occurs twice in the Hebrew list and is retained twice.
“Like an army of God” preserves the Hebrew comparison, which conveys extraordinary size or strength.
vocabulary: Peace
Hebrew shalom can include safety, well-being, and a sound relationship; the repeated peace belongs to Amasai’s pledge.
Whole heart
Undivided commitment, connected here with the shared decision to make David king.

notes: The object of “seek” can be heard as the ark or, through it, God. The draft keeps the ark as the immediate referent.
Chidon is the threshing floor’s name here; 2 Samuel 6:6 has Nacon. The verb about the oxen may mean they stumbled or caused the ark to slip.
Perez-uzza means “outbreak against Uzza,” echoing the verb in David’s reaction.
vocabulary: Cherubim
Heavenly beings associated with the divine throne and the ark; the plural of cherub.
Ark
The sacred chest associated with God’s covenant and presence among Israel.

notes: Huram follows the Hebrew read form; the written form is Hiram.
Elpelet, Beeliada, and Eliphelet are retained as this list gives them.
Baal-perazim is linked to “breaking through,” like the force of water bursting out.
The tree called baka is not certainly identified; balsam is a traditional identification.
This account reads Gibeon, whereas 2 Samuel 5:25 reads Geba.
vocabulary: For the sake of his people
The verse states the benefit to Israel as the reason for the kingdom’s elevation.
Seek guidance
David asks again rather than assuming the earlier battle instruction applies unchanged.

notes: “You did not carry it” supplies the action implied by the Hebrew’s incomplete opening clause.
Ben is present in the Hebrew list. It can also mean “son”; its place here is uncertain.
Alamoth and sheminith are musical directions whose exact performance meanings are lost. Alamoth is related to young women; sheminith to “eighth.”
The Hebrew massa can mean carrying or burden and can also be associated with an utterance. The draft understands Chenaniah’s role musically in this context; directing the carrying is another reading.
vocabulary: Consecrate
Set apart for sacred service, including the required preparation.
Ephod
A garment associated with priestly service; David’s is described as linen.

notes: The food term rendered “portion of meat” is uncertain; a date cake or another food portion has also been proposed.
Jeiel appears twice in the list, as in the Hebrew.
The song has close parallels in Psalms 105, 96, and 106. Its own wording is retained, including Israel in verse 13, the command “Remember” in verse 15, and joy in verse 27.
“In holy splendor” may refer to sacred beauty or to holy attire.
The Hebrew shifts to “their relatives” and names Obed-edom twice. It is unclear whether two men of that name are meant. Jedithun is the form here; Jeduthun occurs nearby.
vocabulary: Covenant
A binding relationship expressed through commitments; the song connects it with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the land.
Faithful love
Hebrew hesed: enduring loyalty and kindness within a relationship.

notes: Chronicles gives a direct statement that David will not build the house; the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:5 is framed as a question.
House moves from a building to a lasting family or dynasty. Verse 14 says “my house” and “my kingdom,” emphasizing God’s claim.
The final Hebrew phrase is difficult. “A man of high standing” is one reading; the wording may concern an elevated human order or station.
“Revealed” renders the image of uncovering someone’s ear.
vocabulary: LORD of Armies
A divine title presenting the LORD as commander of heavenly and earthly forces.
Father and son
The relational language of the royal promise; its wording is retained without adding a later doctrinal interpretation.

notes: The subject of the movement toward the Euphrates is not named again in Hebrew. The draft understands it as Hadadezer.
The figures here differ from the parallel in 2 Samuel 8:4. The Hebrew says a hundred chariots were left; enough horses for those chariots is supplied.
“Forces” supplies the missing object of “stationed.”
Abimelech and Shavsha are retained as named here rather than replaced with forms from parallel lists.
vocabulary: Tribute
Payment acknowledging another ruler’s dominance.
Sea
The name of the great bronze basin later installed at the temple.

notes: Chronicles says the men were shaved; the half-beard detail in Samuel is not supplied.
Chronicles’ chariot and troop figures are retained even where they differ from 2 Samuel 10.
“The River” is the Euphrates. Shophach is the commander’s name here.
vocabulary: Faithful kindness
Hesed here describes loyalty shown between rulers.
Talent
An ancient unit of weight used for large quantities of precious metal; it is not a modern coin.

notes: “Their king” renders malkam; the same consonants can name the Ammonite god Milcom. The text does not explain how the heavy crown was worn.

The verb is difficult. The draft retains the reading that the captives were cut with tools. Another interpretation understands forced labor with saws and iron tools. The harm must not be concealed whichever reading is adopted.
This account explicitly names Lahmi as Goliath’s brother; the difficult wording of 2 Samuel 21:19 is not imported here.
vocabulary: Rephaim
A group associated in biblical tradition with ancient people of exceptional stature.
Weaver’s beam
A heavy wooden part of a loom, used as the comparison for the spear shaft.

sections.18: An altar at Ornan’s threshing floor

notes: Satan can be read as a name or as “an adversary.” Chronicles’ wording differs from 2 Samuel 24:1, which attributes the incitement to the LORD.
The totals differ from 2 Samuel 24:9; Chronicles also states that Levi and Benjamin were not counted.
The narration retains both the beginning of destruction and the LORD’s relenting; it does not supply a timeline to remove the tension.
The price here is six hundred shekels of gold for the site. Samuel gives fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen; the difference remains visible.
vocabulary: Seer
A person receiving divine revelation, a title related to prophetic sight.
Sackcloth
Coarse cloth worn in mourning, distress, or repentance.

notes: Resident foreigners are gathered and assigned work. The account does not describe this labor as a voluntary gift.
Solomon, Hebrew Shelomoh, echoes shalom, “peace.” The promise also repeats the word rest.
The Hebrew gives a hundred thousand talents of gold and a million talents of silver. These very large quantities are retained without reduction.
vocabulary: For my name
The house is dedicated to the LORD’s identity and presence.
Sanctuary
A place set apart as holy for worship and service.

notes: The chapter first counts men thirty and older, then gives twenty and older under David’s final instructions. Both thresholds are preserved.
Shelomith follows the read form in verse 9. Zina in verse 10 and Zizah in verse 11 are both retained.
The Hebrew may mean Aaron was consecrated as most holy, or that he was set apart to consecrate the most holy things. The draft takes the latter reading.
The term for the “mixed offerings” refers to a prepared grain dish, but the precise cooking method is uncertain.
vocabulary: Gatekeeper
A person responsible for controlled access and guarding sanctuary property.
New moon
The beginning of a lunar month, marked by prescribed offerings.

notes: The Hebrew repeats “selected” in the Ithamar clause. The precise drawing procedure is uncertain; a two-to-one alternating mechanism is not added.
The opening is incomplete. The parallel at 23:19 identifies this group as Hebron’s sons, with Jeriah first; the draft does not make Jeriah the father of the other three.
Beno can be read as a name or as “his son.” The relationship of Jaaziah to the surrounding Merarite list is unclear.
vocabulary: Lot
An object or procedure used to assign a choice without an individual selecting the outcome.
Abijah
The eighth priestly division; the same division name appears in Luke 1:5.

notes: The text says six sons but names five. Shimei, named in verse 17, is often supplied here; this draft leaves the written list intact.
Heman’s fourteen sons and three daughters are all mentioned. Some of the final names resemble phrases of praise, but the roster presents them as names.
“Raise his horn” is an image of strengthened standing or honor; whose horn is meant is not explicit.
The first lot has a shorter entry than the later ones. The draft does not insert an explicit twelve-person total there.
Izri, Jesharelah, Azarel, and Shubael differ in form from names in the opening list. They are retained in their respective entries.
vocabulary: Prophesy
Speak or perform under divine inspiration; here the verb describes musical thanksgiving and praise.
Teacher and learner
Skill and training do not exempt a musician from the shared lot procedure.

notes: Asaph is retained here; a related genealogy gives Ebiasaph in 9:19.
The attachment of “his relatives” is uncertain; the draft does not assign an unstated father to Elihu and Semachiah.
Shuppim is retained in this difficult line; it may reflect a textual problem.
Parbar is an uncertain architectural term, perhaps a colonnade or an area adjoining the court.
The Hebrew has Ahijah; an ancient Greek reading instead refers to “their relatives.”
Shelomith follows the read form in verse 25; Shelomoth in verse 26 and Shelomith in verse 28 remain as given.
vocabulary: Dedicated gifts
Property set apart for sacred use.
Outside duties
Administrative and judicial service beyond the sanctuary itself.

notes: Asahel and his successor Zebadiah are both listed; the roster spans more than one point in time.
Elihu is named as David’s brother here; the draft does not replace the name with Eliab.
Gad and Asher are absent from this roster; entries for them have not been supplied.
Shirtai follows the Hebrew read form; the written form gives Shitrai.
Uncle is the ordinary sense of the kinship term here, though the identity of this Jonathan is debated.
vocabulary: Division
An organized group assigned a turn of service.
Chronicles
Records of events or annals; the phrase here names a royal record, not necessarily the biblical book’s title.

notes: The word for court officials can also mean eunuchs; their bodily status is not specified here.
The Hebrew ruach can mean spirit or mind. The draft understands the plan as received through the Spirit; “what he had in mind” is another possible reading.
The cherubim are described as a chariot. The throne image is retained rather than reduced to decoration.
The verse connects written plans with the LORD’s hand and David’s understanding, without spelling out the process of transmission.
vocabulary: Footstool
An image linking the ark with God’s kingship.
Atonement cover
The sacred cover of the ark, traditionally also called the mercy seat.

notes: Several ancient stone names are uncertain. Onyx, dark stones, colored stones, and marble are approximate identifications.
Darics are Persian gold coins. The narrator uses a term from a later period; it is not replaced with a presumed coin of David’s time.
“Our father” may attach to Israel, the ancestor Jacob, or be heard as an address to God. The draft keeps it beside Israel.
The Hebrew says “there is no hope”; the shadow and temporary-resident images frame this as human life’s lack of permanence.
The same bowing gesture is directed toward the LORD and the king. The verse does not make them equals.
“A second time” is explicit; compare the earlier installation in 23:1.
vocabulary: Consecrate
The Hebrew image is “fill the hand,” a phrase associated with committing someone to sacred service.
Palace
Birah can describe a palace or citadel; here it names the temple as God’s royal dwelling.
